Ein, mein, kein + adjetivo, passo a pass: Ein, mein, kein + adjective, step by step
PASSO 1: «ein», «eine», «mein», «kein»…: STEP 1: «ein», «eine», «mein», «kein»… fail to show the case in THREE places: masculine nominative («ein»), neuter nominative («ein») and neuter accusative («ein»). In those places the ADJECTIVE takes over and shows the case: «ein großer Mann» (-er, like the -r of «der»), «ein kleines Kind» (-es, like the -s of «das»). STEP 2: everywhere else, the article already shows the case, and the adjective takes «-e» or «-en», just as after «der»: «eine kleine Frau», «einen großen Mann». STEP 3: nominative: ein großer Mann (-er), eine kleine Frau (-e), ein neues Auto (-es), meine neuen Autos (-en). STEP 4: accusative: einen großen Mann (-en), eine kleine Frau (-e), ein neues Auto (-es), meine neuen Autos (-en). STEP 5: rule of thumb: «-er» and «-es» appear only when «ein» has no ending: masculine nominative, and neuter nominative and accusative.
o português não tem nada parecido. A lóg: English has nothing like this — "a big man", "a small child". The logic is simple, though: German wants the case to show up ONCE. If the article (ein) didn't show it, the adjective does. Think of it as the -r of «der» and the -s of «das» moving onto the adjective: der → ein großeR, das → ein kleineS.

STEP 2: the trick: if the article ends in «-r», «-e» or «-s» (der, die, das), the adjective takes «-e/-en»; if the article has NO ending (ein), the adjective shows the case (-er, -es).
